q: In which year did ARPANET become operational?
explain: ARPANET, funded through ARPA of the US Department of Defense, became operational in 1969. 1983 is the year it moved to TCP/IP.

q: ARPANET switched from NCP to TCP/IP on:
explain: The switch from the Network Control Protocol (NCP) to TCP/IP took place on 1 January 1983.

q: Which term correctly describes any participating device or connection point in a network?
explain: Every computer, server, printer, router or switch taking part in a network is a node. Client and server are only roles a node plays.

q: Which layer of the OSI model transmits raw bits as electrical, optical or radio signals?
explain: The Physical layer (Layer 1) is concerned with sending bits as signals over the medium.

q: Which OSI layer handles data representation, compression and encryption-related functions?
explain: Layer 6, the Presentation layer, deals with data format conversion, compression and encryption-related functions.

q: What is the Protocol Data Unit (PDU) of the Data Link layer?
explain: Layer 2 works with frames. Packets belong to Layer 3, segments to Layer 4 and bits to Layer 1.

q: Which sequence correctly shows encapsulation as data moves down the stack?
explain: Data is wrapped as a TCP segment, then an IP packet, then a frame, and finally sent as bits.

q: Which OSI layer is called the end-to-end layer, handling process-to-process communication and port numbers?
explain: The Transport layer (Layer 4) provides end-to-end communication between processes using ports, segmentation and reassembly.

q: In the TCP/IP model, which single layer covers the OSI Application, Presentation and Session layers?
explain: Session and Presentation functions are included in the TCP/IP Application layer, so TCP/IP has no separate layers for them.

q: Which TCP/IP layer corresponds to the OSI Network layer?
explain: OSI Network (Layer 3) maps to the TCP/IP Internet layer, where IP and ICMP work.

q: Which protocol is connectionless and has low overhead, with no built-in guarantee of delivery or ordering?
explain: UDP sends independent datagrams with no handshake, which keeps overhead low but offers no delivery guarantee.

q: Which feature belongs to TCP but not to UDP?
options: Acknowledgements and retransmission of lost data
explain: Both use ports at Layer 4, but only TCP adds acknowledgements, retransmissions and ordering for reliability.

q: Which statement about IP (Internet Protocol) is correct?
options: It sets up a connection before sending
It is a connectionless, best-effort delivery protocol
It works at the Data Link layer
explain: IP delivers packets on a best-effort basis with no end-to-end reliability guarantee; reliability is added by TCP or the application.

q: Which IEEE 802 standard defines Ethernet?
explain: 802.3 is Ethernet. 802.11 is wireless LAN (Wi-Fi), 802.5 is Token Ring and 802.16 is associated with WiMAX.

q: Which IEEE standard is associated with WiMAX broadband wireless access?
explain: 802.16 covers broadband wireless access associated with WiMAX (Worldwide Interoperability for Microwave Access).

q: How many bits are in an IPv6 address?
explain: IPv6 uses 128 bits (16 bytes) written in hexadecimal groups. IPv4 uses 32 bits.

q: A historical Class C IPv4 address has a first octet in the range:
explain: Class C covers 192-223 with a default mask of 255.255.255.0 (/24). Class A is 0-127, B is 128-191 and D is 224-239.

q: Which IPv4 address is the common loopback address of the local host?
explain: 127.0.0.1 is the usual loopback address, and the whole 127.0.0.0/8 block is reserved for loopback.

q: A conventional Ethernet MAC address is written with how many hexadecimal digits?
explain: A MAC address has 48 bits = 6 bytes = 12 hexadecimal digits.

q: At which OSI layer does a MAC address operate?
explain: MAC addresses are used for local-link frame delivery at Layer 2. Calling it a 'physical address' does not place it in the Physical layer.

q: Which protocol finds the MAC address for a known IPv4 address on the local link?
explain: ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) maps a known IPv4 address to its link-layer address. RARP does the reverse and is legacy.

q: Which protocol automatically supplies a host with an IP address, subnet mask, gateway and DNS servers?
explain: DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) provides IP addresses and network settings. DNS only resolves names.

q: Which device is a multiport repeater that sends incoming signals to every other port without MAC learning?
explain: A hub works at Layer 1 and simply repeats signals to all other ports, which is why it is called a dumb device.

q: Which device connects different IP networks and forwards packets using destination IP and a routing table?
explain: A router works mainly at Layer 3, choosing routes and next hops by IP address.

q: A bridge operates at which OSI layer?
explain: A bridge learns MAC addresses and forwards or filters frames at the Data Link layer.

q: What does a modem's name 'modulator-demodulator' refer to?
options: Encoding data onto a carrier and recovering it
explain: Modulation puts digital information onto a carrier signal and demodulation recovers it from the received signal.

q: Which statement about gateways is accurate?
options: Every gateway works at all seven OSI layers
A gateway can translate between differing communication systems
A gateway is always a hub
A gateway works only at the Physical layer
explain: A protocol gateway translates between different systems or formats, and the layers it uses depend on its function.

q: IP spoofing means:
options: Sending packets with a forged source IP address
Changing your own IP via DHCP
Blocking an IP at the firewall
explain: IP spoofing falsifies the source IP of packets. Legitimately changing a setting is not spoofing.

q: Which protocol synchronizes mail stored on the server across several devices?
explain: IMAP accesses mail on the server and keeps folders and status in sync across devices. POP3 mainly downloads messages.

q: MIME is used in email to:
options: Support attachments, multimedia and non-ASCII text
Download mail to a local device
explain: MIME (Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions) defines content formats; it does not send mail by itself.

q: Which protocol transfers files over an encrypted SSH connection?
explain: SFTP (SSH File Transfer Protocol) works over SSH, unlike plain FTP.

q: Which port number is used by HTTPS?
explain: HTTPS uses port 443. HTTP uses 80 and SMTP uses 25.

q: Which pair correctly matches protocol and well-known port?
explain: SSH uses 22. POP3 uses 110, IMAP uses 143 and Telnet uses 23.

q: Which statement about SSL and TLS is correct?
options: SSL is the modern successor of TLS
TLS is the successor of the obsolete SSL
SSL stands for Secure Socket Link
explain: TLS replaced SSL (Secure Sockets Layer), which is obsolete. TLS gives encryption, integrity and authentication.

q: Which topology uses a single shared backbone, with terminators at both ends in traditional coaxial form?
explain: Bus topology uses one shared backbone, and terminators at the ends prevent signal reflections.

q: How many links does a full mesh of six nodes need, using one link per pair?
explain: Full mesh needs n(n-1)/2 links, so 6 x 5 / 2 = 15.

q: Which network type interconnects LANs in nearby buildings of one organization, such as a university?
explain: A Campus Area Network (CAN) links LANs across nearby buildings such as library, hostel and departments.

q: Which mode allows data to flow in both directions, but only one direction at a time?
explain: A walkie-talkie is half-duplex. Simplex is one way only and full-duplex is both ways at once.

q: Which medium is immune to electromagnetic interference and carries data as light?
explain: Fibre carries light through glass or plastic, so electromagnetic interference does not affect it.

q: In fibre connectors, what does FC stand for?
explain: FC is the Ferrule Connector with threaded coupling; it is not Fibre Channel.
